# References

## Zero reference manager

- Create a `thebibliography` environment in `LaTeX`, which has `\bibitem` entries, specifying the citation key, reference details and the style.
- For example:

```latex
\begin{thebibliography}{9}
\bibitem{texbook}
Donald E. Knuth (1986) \emph{The \TeX{} Book}, Addison-Wesley Professional.

\bibitem{lamport94}
Leslie Lamport (1994) \emph{\LaTeX: a document preparation system}, Addison
Wesley, Massachusetts, 2nd ed.
\end{thebibliography}
```

- This is a manual process, where you have to order, style and write out the references yourself.
- You cite them in the text with `\cite{<citation_key>}`.

## `BibTeX`

- This is essentially a program to generate the bibliography automatically for you.
- You have a `.bib` file, which is a plain text file that contains your bibliography entries in a specific format (e.g. `@book`, `@article`, etc.), with fields for the author, title, year, etc. For example:

```latex
@article{einstein,
    author =       "Albert Einstein",
    title =        "{Zur Elektrodynamik bewegter K{\"o}rper}. ({German})
        [{On} the electrodynamics of moving bodies]",
    journal =      "Annalen der Physik",
    volume =       "322",
    number =       "10",
    pages =        "891--921",
    year =         "1905",
    DOI =          "http://dx.doi.org/10.1002/andp.19053221004"
}

@book{latexcompanion,
    author    = "Michel Goossens and Frank Mittelbach and Alexander Samarin",
    title     = "The \LaTeX\ Companion",
    year      = "1993",
    publisher = "Addison-Wesley",
    address   = "Reading, Massachusetts"
}

@misc{knuthwebsite,
    author    = "Donald Knuth",
    title     = "Knuth: Computers and Typesetting",
    url       = "http://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/\~{}uno/abcde.html"
}
```

- In the text, you cite with `\cite{<citation_key>}` as before.
- Your `LaTeX` engine (e.g. `pdflatex`, `xelatex`) will generate an auxiliary file (`.aux`) that contains the citation keys used in the document (a wish list).
- The program `bibtex` then reads this `.aux` file, looks up the corresponding entries in a bibliography database file (`.bib`), and generates a bibliography file (`.bbl`) that contains the formatted bibliography entries.
- The `LaTeX` engine then basically pastes the contents of that `.bbl` file directly where you have the `\bibliography{<bib_file>}` command in your document, which is where you want the bibliography to appear.
  - These multiple runs are handled automatically by `Overleaf`, as it uses `latexmk` in the background. `Quarto` and `RMarkdown` also handle this automatically when you render the document.
- You can specify the bibliography style with `\bibliographystyle{<style>}`, which determines how the entries are formatted (e.g. `plain`, `alpha`, `abbrv`, etc.).

## `natbib`

- To use `bibtex`, you don't need to load any specific package, but `natbib` is a popular package that provides additional features for handling citations and bibliographies in `LaTeX`.
- Well, the main thing it handles is citation style, really.
  - With `BibTex`, you can only cite using numbers, e.g. `Einstein's theory of relativity [1]`, whereas with NatBib you can cite author-year, e.g. `Einstein's theory of relativity (Einstein, 1905)`.
- You add this to the preamble:

```latex
\usepackage{natbib}
```

- Then cite with `\cite{}`, `\citet{}` (textual), `\citep{}` (parenthetical), etc, and put `\bibliography{<bib_file>}` where you want the bibliography to appear.
- You can customise this further in the premable (the citation style).

## `biblatex`

- The primary issue with `natbib` is that the style of the bibliography is determined by the bibliography style you choose with `\bibliographystyle{<style>}`, and there are only a limited number of styles available and it is (apparently) extremely difficult to create your own custom style.
  - In the background, when you say `\bibliographystyle{plain}`, `natbib` is using a file called `plain.bst` to format the bibliography, and if you want to change the formatting, you have to edit that file, which is a nightmare.
- `biblatex` is a more modern package that provides much more flexibility and control over the formatting of the bibliography and citations.
  - It does not rely on these `bst` files, but rather the formatting is done directly in `LaTeX` with the `biblatex` commands, which is much easier to customise.
- You add this to the preamble:

```latex
\usepackage[style=authoryear]{biblatex}
\addbibresource{<bib_file>.bib}
```

- Then, you cite using `\cite{}`, `\textcite{}` (textual), `\parencite{}` (parenthetical), etc, and put `\printbibliography` where you want the bibliography to appear.
- It is also much faster than `bibtex`.

# Quarto/RMarkdown versus Overleaf

- You control the `R` environment fully, so can install packages, use any version of `R`, etc.
- No compile time limit. 
- Will need to set up `LaTeX` locally.
- Easiest to do this with the `tinytex` package in `R`, which provides a lightweight distribution of `LaTeX` that is easy to install and manage:

```{r}
#| eval: false
install.packages("tinytex")
tinytex::install_tinytex()
```

Beyond basic alignment with amsmath, there are several "pro-tier" behaviors and alternative environments you'll likely run into when your math gets more complex.

1. The "Star" Versions (Unnumbered Equations)
By default, environments like equation and align automatically number your math on the right side of the page.

How to hide numbers: Append an asterisk (*) to the environment name, like \begin{align*} ... \end{align*}.

The amsmath benefit: While standard LaTeX has a displaymath environment, using equation* is generally preferred because it handles spacing more consistently.

2. The cases Environment
If you need to define a function that changes based on a condition (like an absolute value or a piecewise function), cases is the easiest tool.

f(x)={ 
x
−x
​
  
if x≥0
if x<0
​
 
3. Matrices and Grouping
The amsmath package provides specialized environments for matrices that handle the brackets for you:

matrix: Plain numbers.

pmatrix: Parentheses (…).

bmatrix: Square brackets […].

vmatrix: Determinant bars ∣…∣.

4. Text inside Math
If you type "if" or "where" inside a math environment, LaTeX treats it as a string of variables and removes all spacing (looking like if). Use the \text{...} command to insert normal text with proper spacing inside your equations.

To include readable text within math environments, the \text{} command is required to prevent LaTeX from formatting words as italicized variables.

Custom Gem
Gemini said
Yes, the cases environment is a core feature of the amsmath package. While amsmath is the "must-have" foundation for almost any technical document, it is usually part of a small "starter pack" of math packages you'll want to load by default.

1. Using the cases Environment
The cases environment is used for piecewise functions. It automatically adds a large left brace and handles the internal alignment.

Syntax Example:

Code snippet
\[
f(x) = 
\begin{cases} 
  \frac{1}{x} & \text{if } x \neq 0 \\
  0           & \text{if } x = 0 
\end{cases}
\]
The & symbol: Used to align the conditions (like the "if" statements).

The \\ command: Used to start a new line within the brace.

The \text{} command: Essential for writing the "if" part so it doesn't look like italicized variables.

2. Is amsmath the only package you need?
While amsmath is the most important, most users load a "Big Three" set of packages to cover all bases:

amsmath: For the logic, environments (like align, cases), and basic symbols.

amssymb: Provides a massive library of mathematical symbols (like R for real numbers or ℏ).

amsfonts: Provides specialized fonts, such as "blackboard bold" used in set theory.

The Modern Pro-Tip: Many power users now load mathtools instead of amsmath. It automatically loads amsmath but adds fixes for spacing and extra commands like \xRightarrow or better vertical alignment for matrices.

/QA [The cases Environment and Math Packages]
Source Text: The cases environment is part of the amsmath package and is used for piecewise functions. It utilizes the & symbol for alignment and \\ for line breaks. For a complete math setup, users often load amsmath, amssymb, and amsfonts. The mathtools package is a common alternative that includes amsmath while providing additional formatting fixes.
